Stage 3 · Language

Agreeing, disagreeing, and building an essay

Two sets of phrases: one for the room, one for the page.

Read these three replies to the same statement.
  • I couldn’t agree more.
  • I suppose so.
  • I agree up to a point, but…
Which of these actually disagrees?
In English, an argument is stronger when it admits the other side exists.

This is the capstone lesson, and it rests on a principle that governs both halves of it: acknowledging an opposing view makes your own position more persuasive, not weaker. A discussion turn that begins I see what you mean, but… carries more weight than a flat contradiction, and an essay that presents both sides before concluding is more credible than one that argues only its own case.

Agreement and disagreement in English are graded, and most real discussion happens in the middle of the scale rather than at either end. Full agreement (I couldn’t agree more) and blunt disagreement (I disagree) are the two extremes; between them sit partial agreement (That’s true up to a point), acknowledgement (That’s a good point) and softened disagreement (I’m afraid I disagree, I’m not so sure about that). Learners who only have the two extremes sound alternately servile and aggressive.

The written equivalent is the advantages-and-disadvantages essay, and its shape is fixed and expected: an introduction that frames the question without answering it, one paragraph for each side with comparable weight, and a conclusion that weighs them and commits. Presenting one side in two sentences and the other in two paragraphs is not a balanced essay, however even-handed the language sounds.

The most common failure comes at the very end. An essay that concludes There are advantages and disadvantages has not concluded anything — it has restated the title. The closing move in English is to take a position: On balance…, All things considered…, and then say which side wins and why.

Before you look at the table: the tables below grade the agreement and disagreement phrases from strong to weak, then give the essay skeleton. Notice the linking words: although takes a clause, despite takes a noun.

On the page — the essay phrases
The moveWhat you write
Opening the two sidesOn the one hand… · On the other hand…

Spoken and written are not the same set. I couldn’t agree more belongs in a conversation; On balance belongs in an essay. Mixing them is the commonest register error at this level.

Weak agreement is often disagreement. I suppose so and You might be right tell the other person you are not convinced. That is useful when you want to move on, and misleading when you do not.

Rubbish! is in the recording for a reason, and it is a warning. It is genuinely very strong — fine between friends arguing about a car, wrong in a meeting, in a class, or with anybody you have just met.

An essay conclusion should narrow the question, not repeat it. “There are advantages and disadvantages” is not a conclusion. “The case for a full ban is weaker than the case for limiting it” is.

Full grammar reference — agreeing, disagreeing, and the advantages-and-disadvantages essay

What it is

The capstone functional set. Agreeing and disagreeing covers the full range from I completely agree to I’m afraid I disagree, including the partial agreement that carries most real discussion. Essay structure supplies the written equivalent: a balanced argument organised into introduction, one side, the other side, and a conclusion that weighs them.

What it means, and what it does

Both halves rest on the same principle: in English, an argument is stronger when it acknowledges the other side. A discussion turn that begins I see what you mean, but… is more persuasive than a flat contradiction, and an essay that presents both advantages and disadvantages before concluding is more credible than one that only argues its own case. Balance is not weakness; it is the expected shape.

When and why we use it

This is the capstone lesson, and it rests on a principle that governs both halves of it: acknowledging an opposing view makes your own position more persuasive, not weaker. A discussion turn that begins I see what you mean, but… carries more weight than a flat contradiction, and an essay that presents both sides before concluding is more credible than one that argues only its own case.

Agreement and disagreement in English are graded, and most real discussion happens in the middle of the scale rather than at either end. Full agreement (I couldn’t agree more) and blunt disagreement (I disagree) are the two extremes; between them sit partial agreement (That’s true up to a point), acknowledgement (That’s a good point) and softened disagreement (I’m afraid I disagree, I’m not so sure about that). Learners who only have the two extremes sound alternately servile and aggressive.

The written equivalent is the advantages-and-disadvantages essay, and its shape is fixed and expected: an introduction that frames the question without answering it, one paragraph for each side with comparable weight, and a conclusion that weighs them and commits. Presenting one side in two sentences and the other in two paragraphs is not a balanced essay, however even-handed the language sounds.

The most common failure comes at the very end. An essay that concludes There are advantages and disadvantages has not concluded anything — it has restated the title. The closing move in English is to take a position: On balance…, All things considered…, and then say which side wins and why.

Typical situations

You need this for meetings, debates, discussion threads and interviews, and for any piece of argued writing — including the essay you will produce at the end of this lesson and the level.

  • Agreeing completely — the strongest forms.I completely agree. · That’s exactly what I think.
  • Agreeing partially — concede, then qualify — the commonest move of all.I see what you mean, but it doesn’t apply everywhere.
  • Disagreeing politely — softened, with a reason attached.I’m afraid I disagree — the figures suggest otherwise.
  • Acknowledging a good point — before you move on.That’s a good point. I hadn’t thought of that.
  • Introducing an essay — frame the question without answering it yet.Advertising is often accused of manipulating us. This essay will consider both sides.
  • Presenting one side — the advantage paragraph.One major advantage is that advertising funds free services.
  • Presenting the other side — the disadvantage paragraph.On the other hand, a significant drawback is that…
  • Conceding within an argument — although, while, however.Although some adverts do raise awareness, most simply sell.
  • Concluding — weigh, then state a position.All things considered, the benefits outweigh the drawbacks.

How it differs from similar structures

although / while + clause · despite / in spite of + noun or -ing. Although the cost is high… = Despite the high cost…
However, (adverb, starts a new sentence) · but (conjunction, joins clauses) · on the other hand (adverbial, introduces the opposite side of a balanced argument). They are not freely interchangeable in writing.

How to build it

Partial agreement: I see what you mean, but + clause  ·  That’s a good point. However, + clause
Polite disagreement: I’m afraid I disagree (because) + clause
Essay shape: introduction → advantages → disadvantages → conclusion
Balancing: On the one hand, … On the other hand, … However, … In conclusion, …
Strong agreementI completely agree. · I couldn’t agree more. · Absolutely.
Partial agreementI see what you mean, but… · That’s true up to a point. · I agree to some extent.
Polite disagreementI’m afraid I disagree. · I’m not so sure about that. · I’d have to disagree.
Asking for the other viewWhat do you think? · Would you agree with that?
Essay — introductionIt is often argued that… This essay will look at both the advantages and the disadvantages.
Essay — advantageOne major advantage is that… · Another benefit is that…
Essay — disadvantageA significant drawback is that… · On the other hand,…
Essay — concessionAlthough…, · While it is true that…, · However,…
Essay — conclusionIn conclusion,… · All things considered,… · On balance,…

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Agree is a verb and takes no be: I agree, I don’t agree — never I am agree. This error survives to C1 in many learners and is worth eliminating now.
  • I couldn’t agree more means total agreement. The negative form is what makes it emphatic.
  • However is an adverb and takes a comma or a semicolon, not a bare comma splice: …free services. However, they collect data. But is a conjunction and joins two clauses directly.
  • Although and while introduce a clause; despite and in spite of introduce a noun or -ing: Although it is expensive vs Despite the cost. Mixing these is a frequent essay error.
  • In a balanced essay, keep the two sides in separate paragraphs and give them comparable weight. Two sentences for one side and two paragraphs for the other is not a balanced essay.
  • The conclusion must state a position. An essay that ends There are advantages and disadvantages has not concluded anything — use On balance or All things considered and then commit.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I am agree with you. → I agree with you.Agree is a verb and takes no be.
  • I am not agree with this idea. → I don’t agree with this idea.The negative takes don’t.
  • Despite the adverts are funny, they still sell something. → Although the adverts are funny, they still sell something.Despite takes a noun or -ing, not a clause.
  • In conclusion, there are many advantages and disadvantages. → In conclusion, the advantages clearly outweigh the disadvantages.A conclusion must state a position.
  • I couldn’t agree more, but I think you’re wrong. → I see what you mean, but I think you’re wrong.I couldn’t agree more means complete agreement.
  • On the one hand it is cheap, on the other hand it is cheap too. → On the one hand it is cheap; on the other hand, the quality is poor.The two hands must present opposite points.

More examples in context

  • strong agreementI couldn’t agree more — that advert stayed with me for weeks.
  • partial agreementThat’s a fair point, but not every campaign is that responsible.
  • polite disagreementI’m afraid I disagree. Most adverts are designed to sell, not to inform.
  • acknowledgingI see what you mean. I hadn’t thought about the funding side.
  • essay introductionIt is often argued that advertising manipulates consumers. This essay will consider both sides.
  • advantageOne major advantage is that advertising pays for services people use free of charge.
  • second advantageAnother benefit is that public service campaigns can change dangerous behaviour.
  • disadvantageOn the other hand, a significant drawback is that adverts create needs that did not exist.
  • concessionAlthough some campaigns clearly do good, they are a small minority.
  • conclusionAll things considered, the drawbacks outweigh the benefits, and tighter regulation is justified.

A tip for remembering it

For discussion, use the two-part move every time: concede, then object. That’s a fair point, but… For the essay, plan four paragraphs before you write a word: introduce the question, give two advantages with examples, give two disadvantages with examples, then weigh them and commit. If your conclusion could be swapped into any other essay, it is too vague.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Agree takes no be: I agree, I don’t agree.
  2. I couldn’t agree more = complete agreement.
  3. Disagree in two parts: concede, then object.
  4. Although / while + clause; despite / in spite of + noun or -ing.
  5. Give both sides separate paragraphs of comparable weight.
  6. End with a position, not a summary of both sides: On balance… / All things considered…

Stage 5 · Main input

An advantages-and-disadvantages essay

Read it as a writer. This is the last thing you will write at this level.

Before you read: what makes an essay about two sides worth reading?

Choose one. The model does three of these deliberately.

Should advertising to children be banned?

Advertising aimed at children is banned in Sweden and in Quebec, and almost unrestricted nearly everywhere else. That difference suggests the question is genuinely difficult rather than simply unpopular.

One major advantage of allowing it is money. Children’s television, free games and a great deal of what appears online are paid for by advertisers rather than by families, and a ban moves that cost somewhere else. It is worth being aware of who pays when advertising disappears: usually the parent, and usually the poorer parent hardest. There is also an argument about learning. Children who grow up seeing advertising can be taught to recognize it, whereas children protected from it entirely meet the same techniques for the first time at eighteen, with money of their own.

A significant drawback, however, is that the youngest children cannot do this at all. Research consistently finds that below about the age of eight, children do not reliably distinguish an advertisement from a programme. Whatever the benefit to the industry, an audience that cannot see what is being done to it is not being persuaded — it is being used.

The second disadvantage is pressure. Advertising works partly by making a product feel necessary, and a child who wants what the others have does not weigh the household budget first. From the parent’s perspective, the argument arrives at home, and the advertiser is not in the room for it.

On balance, the case for a full ban is weaker than the case for limiting one. Restricting advertising aimed at the youngest children deals with the clearest drawback, while keeping the funding that pays for what older children actually use.

What the model does, in five moves
  • Opens by proving the question is contested — two places, two different laws. No introduction about how important advertising is.
  • Gives the strongest version of the side it will not take. The money argument is made properly before it is answered.
  • Uses evidence where it has it, and says about and consistently rather than pretending to more precision than exists.
  • Names whose view each point belongs to — the industry, the parent — instead of asserting what is simply true.
  • Narrows the question in the conclusion. Not “both sides have a case” but “this specific ban, not that one, and here is why”.
